lit.\u0027\u003cdiv class=\"eqline\"\u003e\u:
'
Positionx = x₀ + v₀·t + ½·a·t²
Velocityv = v₀ + a·t
Timelessv² = v₀² + 2·a·Δx
'
lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003eDos autos salen a la:
'

Two cars leave at the same time from opposite ends: A from x = 0 at 12 m/s and B from x = 110 m at −10 m/s. They meet when xA(t) = xB(t): 12·t = 110 − 10·t → t = 5 s, at x = 60 m. In the x–t graph it is the point where the two lines cross.

'
lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003eEn el \u003cb\u003eMR:
'

In uniform motion the velocity does not change: x = x₀ + v·t. The marks the car leaves every second are evenly spaced. In the x–t graph the motion is a straight line whose slope is the velocity; in the v–t graph it is a horizontal line.

'

'

With constant acceleration: v = v₀ + a·t and x = x₀ + v₀·t + ½·a·t². Starting from rest with a = 2 m/s², the velocity rises 2 m/s every second and the marks spread further and further apart. The x–t graph is a parabola and the v–t graph a line whose slope is the acceleration. The area under v–t is the displacement.

'
lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003eLa velocidad es un \u:
'

Velocity is a vector: it has magnitude (speed) and direction. If the object moves towards smaller x, its velocity is negative and the x–t line goes down. Speed is always positive: here the car moves at 9 m/s, but its velocity is −9 m/s.

'
lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003ePara describir un mov:
'

To describe a motion we choose a reference frame: an origin (x = 0) and a positive direction. The position x tells where the object is and the displacement Δx = xf − xi how much it changed. The distance travelled is the length of the path: they are equal if the object does not turn back.

'
lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003eSi la aceleración tie:
'

If the acceleration points opposite to the velocity, the object slows down. At 20 m/s (72 km/h) with a = −4 m/s² it stops at t = v₀/|a| = 5 s, after travelling d = v₀²/(2|a|) = 50 m. Doubling the speed makes the braking distance four times longer: that is why speed limits matter.

'
